query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the post‐deposition annealing temperature promotes the formation of a coherent, adherent oxide tribofilm on the FeNiCrCoCu coating, which in turn shields the near-surface microstructure from cyclic shear stresses during high-temperature sliding, thereby reducing overall wear and limiting microscopic plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate in its as-deposited condition.
generation.intervention: Apply post-deposition annealing at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600 °C, 750 °C, and 900 °C) in a controlled (atmospheric) environment to deliberately promote oxide tribofilm formation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests conducted in air at temperatures at or above 600 °C under repeated cyclic loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a near-surface oxide/spinel tribofilm that stabilizes grain boundaries and limits dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: The protective oxide tribofilm reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and shear stress during sliding, thereby inhibiting the activation of multiple deformation mechanisms (such as dynamic recrystallization and dislocation pile-ups) that contribute to wear and microscopic plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (unannealed) coating, annealed coatings with a well-developed oxide layer are expected to show lower wear rates, reduced friction coefficients, and diminished evidence of subsurface plastic deformation under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without any post-deposition annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically under high-temperature sliding conditions (≥600 °C) in oxidizing environments—conditions under which oxide formation is thermodynamically favored. It may not hold in inert atmospheres or at significantly lower temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxide development, the uniformity of the oxide film, and the interplay between oxide protection and potential grain coarsening during annealing introduce uncertainties regarding the magnitude of the wear reduction and deformation suppression.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FeNiCrCoCu coatings under identical deposition conditions and then subject them to different post-deposition annealing treatments (including an unannealed baseline). Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests (at or above 600 °C) in air. Use surface characterization (e.g., XPS or TEM) to verify the presence and quality of the oxide tribofilm and cross-sectional microscopy (e.g., EBSD) to assess subsurface deformation.
measurements: Thickness and continuity of the oxide tribofilm
Microstructural analysis of grain boundaries and deformation zones
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If coatings with enhanced oxide tribofilm development (as verified by microscopy and surface analysis) do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rates and microscopic plastic deformation compared to the baseline, or if an increase in oxide film formation correlates with no change or even a deterioration in wear performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Earlier tribological studies on high-entropy alloy coatings highlight two recurring themes. First, high-temperature exposure can lead to the formation of protective oxide or spinel tribofilms that significantly reduce wear and friction, as demonstrated for an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA (PMC7515071). Second, nanocrystalline or fine-grained coating structures—especially after post-deposition treatments—sustain high hardness and improve interfacial stability during sliding, as shown for a CuMoTaWV thin film (PMC7304825). These efforts reveal that oxide layer development and microstructural tuning both influence high-temperature wear performance, yet the exact mechanistic linkage between oxide-scale formation, microstructure evolution, and macroscopic wear over extended sliding remains insufficiently understood for FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how microstructural features—particularly at grain boundaries and near-surface regions—interact with oxide/spinel tribofilms to control both frictional response and subsurface plasticity in FeNiCrCoCu coatings under cyclic sliding at elevated temperatures. The relative importance of tribofilm formation, material transfer, dynamic recrystallization, and dislocation interaction mechanisms is not yet definitively established or validated by direct experimentation.
decision.lever: Systematically vary post-deposition annealing temperature (e.g., 600–900 °C) and time to promote or suppress the formation of a near-surface oxide tribofilm in a controlled atmosphere. Then perform high-temperature sliding wear tests (≥600 °C) on these different conditions to measure wear rate, friction coefficient, and track substructure via cross-sectional microscopy.
decision.why: Building on prior findings that protective phases can form at elevated temperatures to enhance wear resistance, the most direct way to test whether oxide tribofilm development and related microstructural changes govern high-temperature wear and deformation is to implement a systematic study of how thermal processing influences oxide scale stability, coating hardness, and subsequent tribological response under cyclical loading. A null result—i.e., no correlation between oxide tribofilm formation, microstructure, and improved wear performance—would falsify the hypothesis.
